newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 13.

text.p: A number of police officers are facing court charges or internal disciplinary action, but most have been able to avoid publicity by being given name suppression. Police Commissioner Peter Doone said last August that he was concerned public confidence in police could be undermined by misconduct allegations. But this week he refused repeated requests from The Dominion for comment on incidents involving police officers. Page 1.

A pale, swaying Stephen Lawrence Anderson made an eight-minute appearance in Hamilton District Court on Wednesday to face six counts of murder, eight of attempted murder and one firearms charge. Anderson, 24, the alleged gunman of Saturday's massacre in the small central North Island town of Raurimu, looked gaunt and downcast as he stood in the dock wearing white police-issue overalls. He was flanked by police officers. Page 1.

NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan looked likely to hang on to his job after Prime Minister Jim Bolger quelled speculation on Wednesday that the government was preparing for a by-election in Morgan's Te Tai Hauauru electorate. Parliament has echoed with rumours of Morgan's imminent resignation since the disclosure of his pre-election clothes spendup using Aotearoa Television Network money after he had quit as a director of the station. Morgan's resignation would prompt a by-election. A Labour win would remove the Coalition Government's one-seat majority. Page 1.

Maori broadcasting agency Te Mangai Paho knew last year that Aotearoa Television Network's finances were unsound, but failed to advise the government, a Commerce Ministry report says. On Monday the government decided not to go ahead with funding ATN $4 million -- a U-turn on a decision two weeks earlier. The report from the Commerce Ministry's investigation into Te Mangai Paho and Aotearoa Television was made public on Wednesday and shows there were concerns about the station's finances from day one. Page 2.

Two of the major and most detailed winebox transactions -- the European Pacific-promoted Magnum tax credit deal and the $200 million Bank of New Zealand captive insurance scheme -- were not fully investigated by the Serious Fraud Office. The winebox documents, detailing tax-driven transactions through the Cook Islands in the late 1980s, were first delivered to the office in October 1992 by Auckland businessman Stephen Lunn. During dramatic cross-investigation at the inquiry on Wednesday, John Hicks, office assistant director, investigations, said: "As far as I am aware, the office has never carried out an investigation into the Magnum transaction." Page 2.

Labour leader Helen Clark has dismissed Prime Minister Jim Bolger's state of the nation speech as an arrogant and sanctimonious piece of rhetoric. In particular, she criticised the government's social and economic agenda as doing nothing to stop the cycle of disadvantage that many Maori families were trapped in. "It is galling to hear Bolger talking about what the National NZ First Government will deliver for Maori. Judging on the mess his government has made over the pilot Maori television station, it is difficult to see lasting benefit from any initiatives which he may attempt." Page 2.

Reserve Bank governor Don Brash has disputed a claim that he believes a recession is the only way to contain the exchange rate, but said he would prefer interest rates higher. Alliance leader Jim Anderton said on Tuesday, after Brash had given a private briefing to Alliance MPs, that Brash wanted higher interest rates and believed a lower dollar would be achieved with "private sector adjustments". "In other words, recessions will be the way we fix things," Anderton said. Page 12.

Beef prices in the United States are likely to climb 28 percent by the year 2000 after starting a gradual rise from the end of this year, according to Meat Board forecasts. But the board is not expecting any easing in the high New Zealand dollar. Its bankers are forecasting a steady currency. The beef industry suffered severely in the last year because of the oversupply in the United States, but the board expects the market to improve later this year. However, it said prices would be "constrained" until then. Page 12.

ASB Bank boosted interim after-tax profits by 21 percent despite declining interest margins due to "intense competition". After-tax profit for the six months to December was up 21.4 percent to $40.4 million ($33.3 million for the 1995 period). "The reason we were able to improve profitability against a background of a reduction in interest margins is due to productivity improvement and also growing our market," managing director Ralph Norris said. Page 12.

Transport firm Mainfreight has reported an unaudited bottom-line profit of $4.49 million in the nine months to December, up from $3.78 million in the previous corresponding period. The profits were achieved on consolidated revenue of $122.91 million, up 23.2 percent on the previous comparable nine-month period. Page 12.

Shares distributed by Colonial Mutual when the insurer demutualises later this year would be tax-free in the hands of most New Zealand policyholders, the Inland Revenue Department said on Wednesday. The same tax-free status would apply to the
options to buy shares which would be also distributed, any cash value of a policy arising from the share issue, and the proceeds when the shares are first sold, the IRD said. Page 12.
